results.title: Nvidia H100 GPU rental costs surge 50% in six months as AI demand outpaces supply
highlights:
Renting Nvidia’s workhorse AI chip just got a lot more expensive. The cost of H100 GPU rentals climbed roughly 40% between October 2025 and March 2026, according to data from SemiAnalysis, with average rates jumping from $1.70 per GPU-hour to $2.35 per GPU-hour. And if you want to actually get your hands on a cluster of these chips, you’re looking at 12 to 18 months of waiting.

The price spike represents a sharp reversal from the trend that defined much of 2025, when GPU rental prices dropped more than 60% from their 2023-2024 peaks.

...

Inference workloads and multi-agent AI systems have pushed compute requirements well beyond what the existing supply base can handle. On-demand H100 capacity is effectively sold out across Neoclouds and hyperscalers alike.

Even modest deployments have become hard to secure. Clusters as small as 8 nodes, or 64 GPUs, are increasingly difficult to procure on short notice.

February 2026 saw particularly aggressive price moves, with 15-20% increases recorded in a single month as providers adjusted to the new demand reality.

The broader market for on-demand H100 rentals now spans a wide range, from $2.19 to over $4 per GPU-hour depending on the provider and whether the capacity is reserved in advance or purchased on the spot.

...

Lead times for B200 and GB200 deployments have stretched into mid-2026, with the majority of available 2026 capacity already spoken for.

Some operators have locked in their current H100 contracts at legacy rates, with renewals happening at previously agreed-upon pricing. A few have even extended their commitments through 2028. That kind of four-year contract length was nearly unheard of in cloud GPU markets just 18 months ago.

results.title: The Cloud GPU Price War 2026: Neoclouds vs Hyperscalers
highlights:
Is there a cloud GPU price war in 2026? Yes — but not the one the headlines imply. The real 2026 story is a split market: specialist “neocloud” providers (CoreWeave, Nebius, Lambda, Together AI, RunPod) list on-demand GPUs far below the hyperscalers — a rented H100 starts around $2.89/GPU-hour on a neocloud versus roughly $7–$12/GPU-hour on AWS, Azure, or GCP. Yet reserved, contract, and new Blackwell-generation prices actually rose through the first half of 2026. The war is about who wins list-price comparisons, not about a broad price collapse.

...

TL;DR — The 2026 GPU price war in one glance

- Neoclouds list an on-demand H100 from ~$2.89/hr (RunPod) to ~$3.99/hr (Together AI); Nebius lists $3.85/GPU-hr
- Hyperscaler list prices are far higher: AWS p5 works out to ~$6.88/GPU-hr, Azure ND H100 v5 to ~$12.29/GPU-hr (third-party trackers; not confirmed on primary pages)
- One Aug 2026 report puts neocloud rentals up to 66% below the large incumbent clouds
- But contract prices rose: SemiAnalysis' H100 1-year index climbed from ~$1.70 (Oct 2025) toward ~$2.35/GPU-hr (Mar 2026)
- CoreWeave raised list prices ~25% across SKUs in July 2026 and called capacity “effectively sold out”
- AWS quietly raised H200 Capacity Block prices ~15% on Jan 4, 2026 — reportedly its first EC2 GPU price increase in ~two decades
- Nebius disclosed a capacity auction clearing 15% above its highest-ever Blackwell price
- Net: spot/older-Hopper pricing softened; premium, reserved, and Blackwell pricing firmed or rose

...

At the list-price / on-demand tier, specialist clouds genuinely undercut the hyperscalers by a wide margin — and that gap is the marketing engine driving neocloud growth. At the reserved / contract / newest-silicon tier, prices firmed and in several documented cases rose during the first half of 2026, because premium capacity stayed effectively sold out. SemiAnalysis, which publishes a named-methodology H100 rental index, summarizes the tension bluntly: both “GPU prices are falling” and “GPU prices are rising” are true statements in 2026, depending on the tier (SemiAnalysis, 2026).

...

A Seoul Economic Daily report in August 2026 quantified the aggregate gap: neocloud GPU rentals ran “up to 66% lower” than the large incumbent cloud providers (Seoul Economic Daily, Aug 13, 2026). That is the war — but it's a structural gap (neoclouds strip out managed services, enterprise support, and bundled networking) rather than a month-over-month discounting spiral. The hyperscalers are not chasing neocloud list prices down. They are selling a different product at a premium and, in 2026, mostly raising it.

...

Here is the part that breaks the “prices are crashing” narrative. The single best independent data series on GPU rental pricing — SemiAnalysis' H100 rental index, built from a continuously-collected, composition-resistant weighted mean across hyperscalers, neoclouds, and GPU marketplaces — shows the opposite of a collapse for contract capacity. Its 1-year contract H100 range climbed from roughly $1.70/GPU-hour in October 2025 toward $2.35/GPU-hour by March 2026, with the spot-contract composite index sitting around $2.82/GPU-hour in April 2026 and on-demand capacity marked “sold out” since February (SemiAnalysis H100 index, 2026).

The top of SemiAnalysis' 1-year contract range rose through H1 2026 as premium capacity sold out — the clearest counter-evidence to a broad price war.

Why did premium prices rise into what looked like a glut year? Demand outran the Blackwell ramp. SemiAnalysis attributes the tightness to surging token consumption — agentic and reasoning workloads burning far more tokens per request. For the model-level side of that math, see our LLM inference cost per 1M tokens breakdown. New silicon didn't flood the market with cheap capacity; it mostly sold out at a premium before it shipped. Nebius disclosed a 2026 capacity auction that cleared 15% above its highest-ever price for Blackwell chips (Seoul Economic Daily, Aug 13, 2026).

The genuinely softening tier is spot and older-generation Hopper capacity, where more providers and freed-up older cards did compress prices — a real dynamic, but a narrow one, and one that mostly played out through 2025 rather than as fresh 2026 cuts.

...

On its Q2 2026 earnings call (August 11, 2026), CoreWeave disclosed “an approximately 25% increase across SKUs in response to the current demand environment,” adding that pricing and margins for Blackwell and Vera Rubin SKUs were “setting new highs” while prior-generation SKUs sat at or above prior levels. Management described near-term capacity as “effectively sold out” (CoreWeave Q2 2026 call, via Investing.com). Revenue hit $2.58B, up 112% year over year, on a $104B backlog.

...

AWS raised prices on its H200 EC2 Capacity Blocks by roughly 15% effective January 4, 2026 — p5e.48xlarge reportedly moved from $34.61 to $39.80/hr — without a formal customer announcement, in what multiple outlets described as its first EC2 GPU price increase in roughly two decades of EC2 pricing (GIGAZINE, Jan 7, 2026). Treat the exact figures as multiply-reported rather than primary-confirmed.

...

- Default to neoclouds for raw training/inference compute. If you don't need a hyperscaler's managed stack, a neocloud H100 at ~$2.89–$3.99/hr versus $7–$12 on a hyperscaler is the largest single lever you have.
- Don't assume prices will keep falling. Contract and Blackwell prices rose in H1 2026. If you have predictable, sustained demand, locking a rate now can be cheaper than betting on a decline that the data doesn't support.
- Attack utilization first. A rate cut is worth nothing on an idle GPU. Idle GPU time is the dominant waste in AI infrastructure — and the math on when renting even makes sense is in our self-hosting Llama vs the OpenAI API break-even analysis.
- Use spot / older-Hopper capacity where interruptions are tolerable. That is the one tier where prices genuinely softened; batch, fine-tuning, and stateless inference are good fits.

results.title: Ep.018 - Nvidia and the Compute Wars: What It Means If You Are Building Right Now
highlights:
When I first prepared this episode, the story looked relatively straightforward. Nvidia’s data-centre revenue had reached $51.2 billion in a single quarter, Blackwell demand appeared intense, and GPU rental pricing seemed likely to become steadily cheaper as more capacity arrived.

The first observation has become even more significant. 

Nvidia subsequently reported $75.2 billion in data-centre revenue for its fiscal first quarter of 2027, up 21% quarter on quarter and 92% year on year. This is not simply a company earnings statistic. It shows the scale at which accelerated compute has become foundational infrastructure for the AI economy.

The second observation also holds: 

demand for advanced AI systems remains very strong. But the useful founder lesson is not to treat any single backlog figure or “sold out” headline as a permanent fact. Capacity differs by configuration, region, customer relationship, commitment length and workload profile. 

Supply chains change. 

customer priorities change; 

a chip that is scarce for frontier training may be entirely unnecessary for a production inference workload.

The third observation needs more nuance. 

Compute has not followed a smooth, one-way path towards lower prices. 

Older-generation hardware, marketplace supply, reserved commitments and specialist clouds can create excellent economics. At the same time, premium capacity can tighten quickly when large training runs, agentic products or new model releases absorb supply. The relevant question is therefore not, “ Will GPU prices fall?” It is, “What is the least expensive reliable way to meet our specific quality, latency, privacy and volume requirements?”

...

> At the bottom is rent: use APIs, managed model services, or on-demand compute while testing whether users care. This keeps capital commitment low and lets the team change direction quickly.
> 
> The next step is optimize: select smaller or more efficient models, use batching, caching, routing and quantization, and measure whether latency, quality and cost actually meet the product requirement. Most teams can gain more here than by chasing the next hardware release.
> 
> After that comes commit: reserved instances, capacity agreements, dedicated infrastructure or a managed deployment partner. Move here only when demand is sufficiently predictable that the economic benefit outweighs the loss of flexibility.
> 
> Finally, for a limited set of high-volume, sensitive or latency-critical workloads, there is own or operate: dedicated hardware, on-premises systems or edge deployment. This can be compelling, but only once the operational burden and lifecycle costs are understood.

The mistake is to climb this staircase too early. The opposite mistake is to remain at the expensive, unmeasured rental stage after usage has become stable and large enough to justify change.

results.title: Is There An Inference Glut Coming? - by Rob May
highlights:
The short answer is “probably not” but, the estimates are difficult and so there is a high enough probability that it could happen that it is worth understanding the data you need to watch to see if we do tip into an inference glut. Overall, what probably happens is AI data center power runs tight through 2027, loosens through mid-2028, and never actually gluts — but the average conceals two markets moving in opposite directions.

...

Utilization is the variable that matters. Above 92%, landlords have pricing power and tenants queue. Below 68%, buildings sit empty and leases get impaired. The forecast spends the entire two-year window in between.

...

One term you need. Utilization is what share of built AI capacity is actually running paid work. Data centers are leased like real estate but priced like a commodity. Above roughly 92% utilization, landlords set price. Below roughly 68%, tenants do, and the buildings that cannot compete get written down.

...

Supply more than doubles, but half the pipeline never shows up

Developers have scheduled roughly 120 GW of new global data center capacity for delivery between now and August 2028. Historically about half of scheduled capacity lands on time; the constraint is not money or chips, it is transformers, gas turbines, and utility interconnection queues that now run 24 to 48 months.

Applying a 50 to 60% realization haircut, and stripping out the portion not configured for AI, the fleet goes from 35.6 GW to 78.5 GW of AI compute capacity — a 2.2 times increase in 24 months, arriving into a market that is currently 94% full.

Training is the inelastic block. Frontier labs contract training capacity years ahead and cannot flex it down mid-run. It grows 1.55 times regardless of end demand, soaking up 24 GW of the 2028 fleet before a single customer query is served. If a lab ever does defer a training run, that block collapses and the slack widens fast. That is the real glut trigger.

...

This is the part that matters for positioning. There is no single data center market. There is a market for capacity that can host 130 to 600 kilowatt liquid-cooled racks, and a market for everything older. Nvidia’s new generation delivers several times more output per megawatt than the previous one. A hall full of 2023-vintage chips cannot price against that.

Roughly 4 GW of provisioned capacity goes effectively stranded — not because nobody wants compute, but because that compute costs several times more per unit of output than what is arriving next door. Expect the price collapse in this tranche to begin around Q2 2027, four to six quarters before any softness is visible in aggregate figures. Anyone underwriting the sector off blended vacancy statistics will see it late.

...

– Leading, two quarters — Spot GPU-hour pricing for H100-class capacity. This is the stranded tranche. It cracks before anything else does, and it is publicly quoted.

...

Currently mid-70s against a 40 to 50% historical norm. A reversion toward 55% is the first honest sign the shortage is over.

results.title: Short-term or long-term contracts? Emerging cloud providers and AWS are taking different paths | Bitget News
highlights:
Nebius and CoreWeave are aggressively promoting short-term contracts, claiming that in the context of GPU shortages, a pricing premium of more than double can be achieved, which has driven their stock prices up; meanwhile, AWS is sticking to a long-term contract strategy to secure stable revenues in response to uncertainties in AI investments. Analysts believe that short-term contracts offer flexibility and high prices but lack predictability, while long-term contracts provide stability but may miss out on premium opportunities.

...

According to technology media The Information on August 16, Nebius and CoreWeave both pitched short-term contract business to investors over the past week, stating that amid the current tight supply of GPU computing power and surging demand for AI computation, short-term contracts can command a much higher pricing premium. The stock prices of both companies rose sharply as a result.

...

At the heart of this divergence lies a fundamental choice: Short-term contracts can capture the high-price bonuses of immediate computing demand but sacrifice predictability of future revenues; long-term contracts trade off lower prices for a stable income stream, providing investors greater certainty in a market still facing AI investment bubble risk. Paul Meeks, Managing Director and Head of Technology Research at Freedom Capital Markets, said:

...

Nebius and CoreWeave both state that short-term contracts can be sold at prices far higher than mid- to long-term contracts. Nebius executives revealed that new three to six-month contracts are priced at $40 million to $50 million per megawatt per year on an annualized basis—over double the rate for their one- to three-year contracts.

results.title: Why compute might get 10x+ more expensive in coming years
highlights:
An analysis argues that AI compute prices could rise 10x or more in coming years as frontier labs' revenue grows far faster than their compute supply. Anthropic's revenue reportedly grew 10x year-over-year while lab compute only grows about 3x annually, driven by 1.4x Moore's Law gains, 1.2x new fab construction, and 1.8x AI's share of leading-edge wafer allocation (the latter expected to saturate by 2027). Since margins can't realistically exceed the mid-90s percent and labs are reluctant to shift spend toward inference, the piece concludes compute prices themselves must rise. It cites Google reportedly paying $900 million a month for 110K GPUs from SpaceX, roughly 2x spot price, and spot prices already up 40% since February. A back-of-envelope calculation suggests an H100 running a human-level software engineer at current wages should rent for over $250k a year, about 15x today's spot price, with implications for who can compete for scarce compute and how AI applications get priced. Snapshot

...

Google is reportedly paying about $900 million a month for 110,000 GPUs, a blend of GB200s and GB300s, which works out to roughly 2x the spot price per hour for those chips. This premium reflects the need for secure, reliable, large-scale compute tranches that AI labs require beyond what spot instances can offer, on top of a spot price already up 40% since February. Teams evaluating GPU procurement costs can track real-world compute pricing benchmarks like this via daily.dev.

results.title: H100 Rental Prices Rise by 40%, Splitting the GPU Market | WEEX Crypto News
highlights:
NVIDIA's ($NVDA) one-year rental contract price for the H100 has reportedly increased by about 40% from October 2025 to March 2026. As demand for AI model training and inference grows, the GPU rental market is shifting from a single price structure to one that varies based on contract duration, supply channels, and customer segments.

SemiAnalysis reported on April 2 that the one-year contract price for the H100 rose from $1.70 per hour (approximately 2400 KRW) in October 2025 to $2.35 (approximately 3330 KRW) in March 2026. The report described the increase as 'almost 40%'. The 50% increase mentioned in some headlines was not corroborated by accessible primary data and cross-reports.

The same report explained that on-demand GPU rental capacity is sold out across all GPU types. The H100 and H200 eight- node clusters are also mentioned as being in short supply. Short-term users find it difficult to locate available capacity, while long-term contract holders have a greater incentive to retain existing supplies.

Price indicators do not converge into a single figure. Silicon Data aggregates H100 rental prices separately for NeoCloud and hyperscalers. The current price on the H100 page is listed as $2.53 per hour (approximately 3580 KRW).

The upper index screen of the same platform presented H100 prices as $2.77 (approximately 3920 KRW) for NeoCloud and $7.18 (approximately 10160 KRW) for hyperscalers as of July 30. NeoCloud refers to a group of emerging cloud providers that specialize in renting GPU infrastructure, while hyperscalers refer to large cloud providers.

Another public index, gpurentprice.com, reported the H100 price as $4.57 (approximately 6470 KRW) as of July 29. However, the three indicators differ in contract duration, provider groups, sample composition, and regions, making it difficult to compare absolute prices one-to-one. Even for the same H100, prices vary depending on whether it is on-demand or a one-year contract, and whether it is from NeoCloud or a large cloud provider.

Silicon Data stated in a blog post on August 4 that the NeoCloud price for the H100 rose by 7.0% over 12 weeks, while the H200 increased by 14.4%. The price difference between the H100 and H200 was reported to have widened from 5% to 0.4% and then to 16.2%. This suggests that the demand for AI compute is spreading across multiple GPU generations rather than being limited to a shortage of a specific chip.

There are counterarguments as well. Industry writings have claimed that the median price for on-demand H100 rentals has not significantly changed since March, remaining around $2.73 as of June 2026. The simultaneous observation of a sharp rise in contract prices and stagnation in spot median prices indicates that market conditions should be interpreted with a nuanced understanding of the indicators.

GPU-hour is a cost unit for using one GPU for one hour. AI companies bear this cost directly when training large language models or operating inference services, or it is reflected in cloud fees. When rental prices rise, companies that do not purchase GPUs directly are also exposed to fluctuations in service costs.

results.title: H100 Rental Fees Jump 50% in Six Months-AI Demand Is Squeezing the Whole Stack | AInvest
highlights:
- H100 and Blackwell GPU rental costs surged over 50% in six months, straining AI budgets as demand outpaces supply.

- Market splits between cheap spot pricing and scarce usable clusters, with 4% vs. 99% availability across providers.

- Nvidia’s $2B CoreWeave CRWV-- investment and 2032 service deals highlight persistent premium supply constraints.

- Bears bet on Blackwell/MI300X substitution, but high-end coherent capacity remains scarce for large-scale training.

- Key watchpoints include rental price ceilings, cluster economics shifts, and uneven

...

The AI compute squeeze is becoming a budget problem, not just a headline. Blackwell cloud rental jumped to $4.08 per GPU-hour from $2.75 just two months earlier, while H100 1-year contracts rose from $1.70/hr/GPU to $2.35/hr/GPU. That leaves buyers in an awkward spot: demand for training and inference is still strong, but the compute bill is rising faster than many plans accounted for.

...

The bullish read is straightforward: premium capacity is tight. Demand has surged, and on-demand capacity is sold out across all GPU types. The bearish read is also real: the broader H100 market is not uniformly at peak levels, with H100 spot prices collapsed roughly 64% from their 2024 peak and Bloomberg's benchmark for H100 rentals notably below earlier spikes.

The more balanced view is that the cheapest H100 hours may not signal a bubble, but the capacity buyers actually need for fast training, low-latency inference, and reliable cluster builds is getting harder to secure. That is where budgets tend to break first.

...

H100 pricing runs from $0.30/hr spot to $3.70/hr on average. That spread shows cheap units exist, but usually under more constrained conditions. Spot discounts, looser SLAs, location trade-offs, or lower reliability can make the listed price look attractive right up until a job needs stability.

When a usable cluster depends on matched 8-GPU nodes, networking, and consistent availability, the low end of the market stops being the best benchmark.

...

The availability split is striking. Lambda Labs shows 4% availability across 68 GPU configurations, while RunPod shows 99% availability. Two buyers with the same budget can therefore get very different results: one secures a deployable cluster, the other gets a longer research phase.

That helps explain why premium pricing and pre-allocated capacity can persist even when some vendors still advertise lower numbers. Buyers are paying for predictability, faster fulfillment, and less risk of project delay. In early 2026, on-demand capacity is sold out across all GPU types, and holders of locked capacity are not eager to release it back into the pool.

...

Suppliers with guaranteed access are still acting as if supply remains constrained. Nvidia NVDA-- made an additional $2 billion investment in CoreWeave CRWV-- and had already agreed to buy more than $6 billion in services through 2032. That suggests leading providers are still locking in long-duration demand while capacity remains unevenly distributed.

results.title: David Sacks Warns Of Dark GPU Glut Harming NVIDIA AI Financing
highlights:
David Sacks, a prominent advisor to former President Trump and a member of the President’s science and technology advisory council, expressed concerns regarding the oversupply of compute power as a potential stumbling block for this initiative. In his discussion on the All In Podcast, Sacks stated that the most pressing risk does not stem from dwindling demand. Instead, he warned of an impending oversupply that could mirror the dark fiber phenomenon following the dot-com bust, where extensive infrastructure investment failed to yield returns.

“The biggest risk, to me, is not on the demand side,” Sacks explained. “The biggest risk is that you get a glut of compute and you get an overbuild.” Such an oversupply could severely impact stakeholders, especially if investments were made under inflated expectations of $30 to $50 per watt for compute power.

As tech giants ramp up their investment in data center infrastructure, Sacks believes the very political opposition to AI data centers might inadvertently protect against an oversupply. He notes that the hurdles associated with building new facilities serve to moderate the market. “All of a sudden, there are too many people racing to supply this compute and now there’s an oversupply. That’s the risk factor. In a weird way, all of the political headwinds ensure against that outcome,” he said.

The financial implications of NVIDIA’s venture are staggering; Sacks estimates that Elon Musk could potentially generate upwards of $500 billion in revenue by providing a gigawatt of compute, assuming his cost assessments hold. However, other industry players, such as the compute infrastructure provider Nebius, have indicated that annual contract values for cloud agreements range from $20 million to $25 million per megawatt, suggesting Musk’s pricing strategy may be at odds with broader market realities.
